blocks.text: The Greek word behind "apostle" is apostolos - a delegate sent with full authority to act on behalf of the one who sent them, while the sender remains behind to back them up. For a Christian, this means God sends them to do what He Himself would do if He went - {{hb 3:1|Hebrews 3:1}}, {{mt 28:19,mt 28:20|Matthew 28:19-20}}, {{mk 3:14,mk 3:15|Mark 3:14-15}}, {{lk 6:13|Luke 6:13}}.

Called missionaries, church planters, and general overseers fall under this ministry. Scripture records twenty-four apostles, the most prominent being our Lord Jesus Christ Himself - {{hb 3:1|Hebrews 3:1}}, alongside the twelve disciples, Paul, Barnabas, Andronicus, James, and others.

The Hebrew word behind "prophet" is navi - one who speaks on God's behalf - {{hb 1:1|Hebrews 1:1}}. Prophets are, first and foremost, preachers of righteousness - {{act 15:32|Acts 15:32}}, though they sometimes foretell what's to come - {{act 11:28|Acts 11:28}}, {{act 21:10|Acts 21:10}}. Prophecy is one of the gifts of the Spirit - {{1co 12:4,1co 12:5,1co 12:6,1co 12:7,1co 12:8,1co 12:9,1co 12:10,1co 12:11,1co 12:28|1 Corinthians 12:4-11, 28}}, and those who exercise it persistently are called prophets. Songs ministers (choristers) and intercessors also fall under this ministry.

Being a prophet, though, goes beyond simply displaying the gift of prophecy - {{1co 14:5|1 Corinthians 14:5}}; it comes alongside supernatural signs - visions, dreams, trances - an inward voice, and an unusual sense of God's presence and power. Scripture names roughly seventy-eight true prophets and prophetesses, among them Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Daniel, Haggai, Deborah, Jonah, and Agabus.

The Greek euangelistes, "evangelist", means one who announces the good news of God's kingdom. Every believer is charged to do the work of an evangelist - {{2tm 4:5|2 Timothy 4:5}}, {{2co 5:18|2 Corinthians 5:18}}, but some are specifically called with the ministry gift of evangelism. Evangelists are mobile ministers, not confined to one location, moving between places to preach the good news of Jesus Christ to those who haven't heard it, often drawing crowds through the strength of a faith that brings signs and wonders.

The Hebrew ra'ah and the Greek poimen, both translated "pastor", mean "shepherd." A pastor's calling is to tend, feed, and guard the flock of God, giving proper attention to people and remaining accessible to them, doing much of the work of counselling, praying, and restoring lost souls - {{jr 3:15|Jeremiah 3:15}}. Pastors must carry the qualities laid out in {{1tm 3:1,1tm 3:2,1tm 3:3,1tm 3:4,1tm 3:5,1tm 3:6,1tm 3:7|1 Timothy 3:1-7}} and live an exemplary life. House fellowship leaders and children's/teenagers' leaders fall under this ministry.

The Greek didaskalos, "master", is used of a teacher in Scripture - a description given to Jesus Himself - {{jo 3:2|John 3:2}}. A teacher is specially called to impart instruction and communicate the knowledge of God's word with an authority as though they were the author of the Bible themselves, illuminating Scripture with revelation and insight, discovering hidden truth, and never boring to listen to.
